definition: Colonization means the act of settling one's own people in another territory and ruling it for the home country's benefit.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word colonization. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know colonization should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Maps tell the story of colonization plainly: within forty years of the first landing, the coast's fishing villages bore the settlers' saints' names and paid their taxes to a crown across the ocean.
Occupation is shallower than colonization: soldiers hold the squares and the ports, but nobody plants a family there, and when they march out little of them remains.
Annexation goes further than colonization: colonization runs a territory as a foreign possession, while annexation erases the line on the map and makes the land legally part of the taker itself.

An occupation holds a territory without taking root in it: troops in the citadel, a curfew at dusk, and no settlers behind them — when the army leaves, little remains. Colonization digs in, planting the outsiders' own people on the land to stay and running the place for their home country.

Annexation is a stroke-of-pen act: the border is redrawn and the territory legally absorbed into the taker's own state. Colonization keeps the land foreign — a possession settled and governed from outside, not a new province of home.

Colonization means the act of settling one's own people in another territory and ruling it for the home country's benefit.
The island of Teralva had traded with the mainland for centuries before the charter ships began its colonization in 1611.

Within a generation everything ran through the newcomers: two thousand mainland families farmed confiscated terraces, the port shipped the whole sugar crop to the mother country at prices fixed there, and island children recited a history that began the day the ships arrived.
Colonization is the full pattern, not just the arrival: outsiders who come to stay, planted on the land itself, and a ledger whose profits sail home.
Teralva was not merely conquered or taxed — it was settled and run as a possession, which is what separates this word from every other kind of takeover.

Colonization is the historian's word for settlement plus control: outsiders who come to stay, and a ledger kept for the home country.

Conquest names only the taking itself — the campaign that wins the land; occupation holds it without rooting; and when power runs on pressure and deference rather than possession, this unit's hegemony is the word.
Scientists borrow the term gently: a species colonizes a habitat when it establishes itself there.

The delta gallery of the maritime museum opens with a single question printed over the door: when does a trading post become something more?
The first cases hold pepper sacks and ledgers — for thirty years, the visiting merchants bought, sold, and sailed away each monsoon.
The turn comes in the third case: a yellowed decree offering free passage and forty acres to any family from the home country willing to farm the delta permanently.
Two display cases later, colonization had remade the shore.
Settler villages ringed the old trading fort, a governor reported to distant directors, and the delta's rice fed the home country's ports.
The final case is the quietest: a schoolbook printed in the settlers' language, its maps still labeling the delta an overseas possession rather than part of any homeland.
